2. **Two-Vehicle Minor Collision (No Injuries):** Fill out the yellow-and-blue **Constat Amiable** (European-style Joint Accident Report) located in your glovebox. Both drivers must sign it. If the other driver refuses or only speaks Darija/Tamazight, do not argue—call the authorities.
3. **Urban vs. Rural Jurisdiction:**
   - **Inside City Limits (*Périmètre Urbain*):** Call **19** (from a local SIM) or **112** (from any mobile) to summon the **Police (Sûreté Nationale)**. A specialized traffic officer (*Constatateur*) will draft an official report.
   - **Outside Cities / Highways / Atlas Mountains:** Call **177** for the **Gendarmerie Royale**.
4. **Parked Damage / Hit-and-Run:** Go to the nearest *Arrondissement de Police* to file a *Déclaration de perte/dégâts contre X* and obtain a stamped receipt (*Récépissé*). Handing this document to your rental agent at drop-off legally activates the underwriter's policy and ensures you walk away paying **0 MAD**.

callout.text: When renting with ZwinCar under our Franchise Zéro package, minor cosmetic parking scuffs under 3 cm and normal road gravel wear do not require a police report—saving you hours of bureaucracy at the end of your trip.

faqs.question: Can I use my premium credit card insurance (Amex, Chase Sapphire, Visa Infinite) in Morocco instead of buying Zero Excess?
faqs.answer: Yes, provided your card explicitly covers Morocco (always check country exclusions) and does not exclude SUVs/4x4s like the Toyota Prado TX. To activate credit card coverage, you must decline the rental agency's Zero Excess (SCDW) and accept Basic CDW. Be prepared: the Moroccan agency will still freeze the full franchise of 10,000 to 25,000 MAD (€920–€2,300) on your card. If damage occurs, the agency charges your card directly, and you must obtain the signed condition report, CMI payment slip, and repair invoice to claim reimbursement from your credit card issuer at home.

faqs.question: What happens if I don't have a credit card and only have a Debit Card (Visa/Mastercard Debit, Revolut, Wise)?
faqs.answer: Standard Moroccan banking terminals (CMI) often reject prolonged pre-authorization holds (empreintes bancaires) of 15,000+ MAD on debit cards, or they execute a direct debit instead of a temporary freeze. However, if you upgrade directly to the rental company's Zero Excess (Franchise Zéro) option, operators like ZwinCar waive the massive credit card hold entirely, allowing you to pay the rental and a negligible security deposit (0 to 3,000 MAD) via debit card or cash.

faqs.question: Does Zero Excess cover windshield chips and flat tires in the Atlas Mountains?
faqs.answer: Standard Zero Excess (Rachat de Franchise) covers all bodywork, bumpers, and mechanical collision damage, but typically excludes glass and tires unless you select the 'Bris de Glace & Pneumatiques' (BGP) add-on. Adding BGP costs roughly 30 to 50 MAD (€3–€4.50) per day and is essential if driving the N9 (Marrakech to Ouarzazate) or N10 routes where loose gravel frequently chips windshields.

faqs.question: How long does it take for a Moroccan car rental deposit pre-authorization to be released?
faqs.answer: When the rental agent cancels the pre-authorization (mainlevée d'empreinte) on the CMI terminal at drop-off and hands you the printed cancellation ticket, the release instruction is sent immediately to the Moroccan acquiring bank. Depending on your international issuing bank (especially in the UK, France, US, or Germany), it takes between 3 and 14 business days for the blocked funds to reappear in your available balance. Always keep the printed 'Ticket d'Annulation' until the hold disappears.

faqs.question: Is off-road driving in Merzouga or Zagora covered if I rent a 4x4 with Zero Excess?
faqs.answer: Driving on unmarked desert sand dunes (Erg Chebbi or Erg Chegaga) is strictly excluded by all Moroccan insurance underwriters, even with a 4x4 and Zero Excess. However, graded gravel access tracks (pistes carrossables) leading to desert camps or Atlas valleys are tolerated when renting an authorized 4WD vehicle like the Dacia Duster 4x4 or Toyota Prado TX, provided you drive at safe speeds and do not cause undercarriage damage from reckless rock crawling.

title: Local Moroccan Rental Agencies vs Brokers (Rentalcars, DiscoverCars): The $8/Day Illusion Autopsy

summaryDirectAnswer: Booking an $8/day car in Morocco via international brokers (Rentalcars, DiscoverCars, BSP Auto) is a loss-leader trap. Because operational break-even for a Moroccan agency is 240 MAD (€22) per day, sub-cost broker bookings trigger forced counter upsells: 15,000 to 25,000 MAD (€1,400–€2,300) credit card blocks, rejected third-party insurance, or 300 MAD/day mandatory waivers. Vetted local Moroccan agencies charge transparent flat rates (280–400 MAD/day) with zero or low deposits (0–5,000 MAD) and direct WhatsApp accountability.

sections.heading: The Unit Economics of a Moroccan Rental Car: Why $8/Day is Mathematically Impossible
sections.content:
When searching for a rental car at Marrakech Menara (RAK) or Casablanca Mohammed V (CMN) on aggregators like DiscoverCars, Rentalcars.com, or BSP Auto, you are routinely presented with base rates of €6 to €9 (65 to 100 MAD) per day for a Dacia Sandero or Kia Picanto. To understand why this rate always results in a confrontation at the airport terminal, you must examine the forensic unit economics of fleet management in Morocco.

A Moroccan car rental agency—whether an international franchise (Green Motion, Goldcar, Surprice) or an independent operator—faces rigid fixed costs dictated by Moroccan automotive financing and regulatory compliance under the Ministry of Transport and Logistics (*Cahier des Charges relatif à la location de voitures sans chauffeur*):

*   **Vehicle Financing (LOA / Crédit-Bail):** A base-model Dacia Sandero Stepway Essential costs 152,000 MAD (€14,000) new in Morocco. Financed over 36 months via commercial leasing (Wafabail, Sogelease) at current Moroccan interest rates (6.5%–8%), the monthly note is roughly 4,400 MAD (€405).
*   **Commercial Multi-Risk Insurance (*Assurance Tous Risques Usage Location*):** Unlike private Moroccan policies costing 4,000 MAD/year, commercial rental fleet insurance mandates between 12,000 and 16,500 MAD (€1,100–€1,520) annually per vehicle due to high claim frequency.
*   **Preventive Maintenance, Tires, and GPS Tracking:** Operating across the High Atlas or coastal highways requires oil changes every 10,000 km, tire replacements every 35,000 km, and mandatory GPS fleet immobilization hardware, adding 700 MAD/month.
*   **Airport Parking & Staff Overhead:** Concessions or shuttle logistics at Agadir Al Massira or Tangier Ibn Battuta, plus staff salaries, add another 800 MAD/month per active unit.

**Total Monthly Break-Even Per Vehicle:** ~7,100 MAD (€655).
Assuming a strong 80% utilization rate (24 rented days per month), **a Moroccan agency loses money the second a car leaves the lot for less than 295 MAD (€27) per day.**

When you book a car on DiscoverCars for €8/day, the broker takes a 25% to 40% commission, leaving the local fulfillment supplier with roughly €5 (54 MAD) per day. The supplier accepts this negative-margin booking for one reason only: the broker voucher delivers a captive customer to their desk at 11:00 PM who has no alternative transport. The counter agent is incentivized—often solely compensated by a 15% to 20% commission on desk upsells—to extract at least 250 MAD/day from you through insurance manipulation, credit card technicalities, or microscopic return damage claims.

callout.text: If your base rental rate in Morocco is under 220 MAD (€20) per day outside of a long-term monthly contract, you are not buying a car rental—you are buying an entry ticket into a high-pressure financial extraction funnel at the airport desk.

sections.heading: The Third-Party Broker Insurance Trap: Why 'Full Coverage' Means Zero Coverage at the Desk
sections.content:
The single greatest point of friction reflected in negative *Rentalcars Morocco reviews* and *DiscoverCars Morocco scam* threads on Reddit and Trustpilot revolves around the "Full Protection" or "Zero Excess" insurance sold during online checkout.

When you pay Rentalcars (Booking.com Group) or DiscoverCars an extra €9 to €14 per day for "Full Coverage," you are **not** buying car rental insurance from the Moroccan agency providing the car. You are purchasing a **third-party reimbursement policy** underwritten by an offshore financial entity (such as Zurich Insurance PLC in Ireland or Cover Genius in the UK). 

Under the Moroccan Insurance Code (*Loi n° 17-99 portant code des assurances*), an offshore broker policy has zero legal standing with the local rental fleet's insurer (Wafa Assurance, Saham/Sanlam, AtlantaSanad, or RMA). Consequently, when you arrive at the desk in Casablanca or Marrakech, the agent will inform you of three non-negotiable realities:

1.  **Your Broker Insurance is Unrecognized Locally:** As far as the Moroccan agency is concerned, you have only basic Collision Damage Waiver (CDW) with a massive deductible (*franchise*).
2.  **The Mandatory 15,000–25,000 MAD Pre-Authorization (*Empreinte Bancaire*):** Because you did not buy the agency's internal Super CDW (SCDW), they must freeze the full excess amount on your physical credit card. For an economy car, this is 12,000 to 18,000 MAD (€1,100–€1,650); for a Dacia Duster or SUV, it reaches 22,000 to 30,000 MAD (€2,000–€2,750).
3.  **The Upfront Cash Liability:** If a scooter clips your wing mirror in the medina of Fes or a rock chips your windshield on the A3 motorway, the local agency will immediately capture 4,000 to 15,000 MAD directly from your blocked deposit.

To recover your money from DiscoverCars or Rentalcars, you must pay the Moroccan agency first, and then submit an exhaustive digital claim packet from home. This packet requires:
*   The original signed rental contract (*Contrat de Location*).
*   The check-in and check-out condition reports (*État des lieux*).
*   An official itemized repair invoice from a registered Moroccan garage showing the *Identifiant Commun de l'Entreprise* (ICE) and VAT (TVA) breakdown.
*   An official police report (*Constat Amiable* or *Procès-Verbal de la Gendarmerie Royale*).
*   Your final credit card statement showing the settled debit.

Here is the forensic catch: predatory budget suppliers rarely repair cosmetic scratches immediately. They pocket the penalty from your deposit and send the car back out. Because they will refuse to provide you with an official fiscal garage invoice (*Facture normalisée avec ICE*)—Instead handing you an arbitrary internal "damage matrix sheet"—the international broker's claims department frequently rejects the reimbursement request for "insufficient fiscal proof of repair cost."

callout.text: Under Moroccan law, any multi-vehicle damage claim requires a formal 'Constat Amiable' filled out at the scene, or a police report. Without this document, both local insurers and international broker policies void all coverage, rendering you 100% liable for the full value of the car.

sections.heading: Credit vs. Debit Card Engineering & CMI Terminal Traps at Moroccan Airports
sections.content:
Even travelers who arrive prepared to let the agency block a 20,000 MAD deposit on their card frequently fall victim to technical rejection at the rental desk—forcing them to forfeit their prepaid voucher or pay 300 to 400 MAD (€28–€37) per day in non-refundable local SCDW insurance.

Moroccan payment infrastructure is governed exclusively by the **CMI (Centre Monétique Interbancaire)**. Understanding how CMI terminals interact with foreign bank cards is critical to surviving a broker pickup:

### 1. The 'CREDIT' Embossing & BIN Check Trap
Around 85% of European (especially French, Belgian, and German) and UK bank cards are technically classified as **Debit** or **Deferred Debit (*Débit Différé*)**, even if the user treats them like credit cards. Furthermore, neo-banks like Revolut, Wise, N26, and Monzo issue strictly prepaid/debit BINs (Bank Identification Numbers). 
Predatory franchise desks at Menara and Mohammed V airports program their SOPs to reject any card that does not physically display the word **CREDIT** on the plastic, or fails a BIN lookup test. Even if you have €10,000 sitting in your Revolut account, a CMI *pré-autorisation* (which locks funds for up to 30 days without settling the transaction) cannot be reliably executed on standard debit rails.

### 2. The Lead Driver Name Mismatch
If the online booking on BSP Auto or Rentalcars was made under the wife's name, and the husband presents his physical credit card for the 18,000 MAD deposit, the agency will legally void the rental agreement. Changing the lead driver name at the desk is prohibited by broker terms; the agency will force you to cancel the broker booking (with zero refund under the 48-hour no-show clause) and open a brand-new walk-in contract at inflated local walk-in rates.

### 3. Dynamic Currency Conversion (DCC) & Charge vs. Block
Some lower-tier desk operators do not perform a standard CMI pre-authorization (*empreinte*). Instead, they run an actual **Sale Transaction (*Vente*)** for 15,000 MAD. When you return the car undamaged 10 days later, they run a refund. 
Why is this catastrophic for the renter? Because your home bank charges a 2.5% to 3% foreign exchange fee on the initial 15,000 MAD debit, and another 2.5% to 3% FX spread on the refund, plus Moroccan CMI interchange variations. You end up losing 900 to 1,350 MAD (€85–€125) in pure currency conversion friction on a "refundable" deposit.

callout.text: Always ask the Moroccan agent to see the CMI terminal screen before entering your PIN. Ensure the transaction type reads 'PRÉ-AUTORISATION' and NOT 'VENTE' (Sale), and always select payment in local currency (MAD), declining the terminal's predatory EUR/GBP/USD conversion rate.

sections.heading: Forensic Comparison: International Brokers vs. Vetted Local Moroccan Agencies
sections.content:
To strip away marketing claims, we audited the real-world financial and operational outcomes of a standard **7-day rental of a Dacia Sandero Stepway (or Renault Clio 5)** during shoulder season in Marrakech.

| Audit Parameter | International Broker (Rentalcars, DiscoverCars, BSP Auto) | Low-Cost Franchise Desk (via Broker Voucher) | Vetted Local Moroccan Agency (Direct / ZwinCar Standard) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Advertised Online Rate** | 85 MAD/day (€8/day) | N/A (Fulfillment Partner) | 300–350 MAD/day (€28–€32/day) |
| **Broker Insurance Add-on** | +120 MAD/day (€11/day) | Rejected at counter | Included / Transparent Tier |
| **Desk Mandatory Upsell (If Card Rejected)** | None mentioned | +280 to 350 MAD/day (€26–€32/day) | **0 MAD** |
| **Security Deposit (*Caution*)** | Stated as 12,000–20,000 MAD in fine print | **15,000 to 25,000 MAD** blocked on Credit Card | **0 to 4,000 MAD** (Cash, Debit, or Credit accepted) |
| **Windshield, Tires & Undercarriage (*Bris de Glace*)** | Covered by reimbursement only | Excluded from base CDW | Explicitly includable for 30–50 MAD/day |
| **Airport Pickup Logistics** | Unclear until voucher issued | Shuttle bus to industrial zone (15–30 min wait) or 2-hour terminal queue | Meet & Greet at terminal exit (P1 Parking) in 10 mins |
| **Cross-Region Support (e.g., Merzouga / Dakhla)** | Call center in Manchester or Riga | Subcontracted tow truck at renter's expense | Direct WhatsApp with fleet manager; local garage network |
| **Real 7-Day Total Out-of-Pocket** | **1,435 MAD** (Online illusion) | **3,400 to 4,200 MAD** (After desk coercion or hubcap claim) | **2,100 to 2,450 MAD** (Fixed, final, zero surprises) |

### The 'Shuttle Bus' Bait-and-Switch
When filtering on aggregators for "In Terminal" at Marrakech (RAK) or Agadir (AGA), many discount suppliers manipulate their location metadata. Morocco's airport authority, **ONDA (Office National Des Aéroports)**, restricts permanent inside-terminal booths to a small handful of legacy operators paying massive concession fees. 

Budget broker partners operate from gas stations (like the Afriquia or Shell stations along the Route de la Ménara in Marrakech or the Route de Nouaceur near Casablanca CMN). You stand outside in 38°C heat waiting for an unbranded Dacia Dokker shuttle van to drive you to a dusty office 4 kilometers away—where you have zero leverage to walk away when they demand a 22,000 MAD deposit.

callout.text: Never sign a Moroccan rental contract that leaves the 'Franchise' (Excess/Deductible) box blank or writes 'Selon Tarif Général' (According to general tariff). Demand the exact numeric figure in MAD be written on the physical carbon-copy contract before taking the keys.

sections.heading: The Return Inspection Autopsy: How Low-Cost Desks Monetize 2cm Scratches
sections.content:
If you successfully navigate the pickup desk with a valid physical credit card, decline the agency's €30/day insurance, and allow them to block 18,000 MAD on your card, your financial risk shifts entirely to the **return inspection (*État des lieux de retour*)**.

Because the agency received only €5/day from the broker for your 7-day rental (€35 total revenue), their entire profit margin depends on finding chargeable damage upon return. Our fleet audits across Casablanca, Tangier, and Marrakech reveal five systematic damage extraction tactics used by ultra-low-cost broker partners:

### 1. The Spare Tire & Jack Swap (*Roue de Secours et Cric*)
When you pick up the car at night, you inspect the bodywork, take a video, and drive off. You rarely lift the trunk carpet to inspect the spare wheel well. Either the spare tire is already missing, or it contains a punctured, shredded tire from a previous renter. Upon return, the agent goes straight to the trunk, opens the floorboard, and charges you **2,500 to 3,500 MAD (€230–€320)** for a missing or ruined Continental tire and OEM jack.

### 2. The Lower Front Bumper & Undercarriage Rub
Moroccan roads feature steep, unpainted concrete speed bumps (*dos d'âne*) at the entrance and exit of every rural town, alongside deep drainage dips in the High Atlas. Even at 15 km/h, the low plastic front lip (*bavette*) of a Renault Clio 5 or Peugeot 208 frequently scrapes. During return, the agent gets on one knee and runs their hand *underneath* the invisible bottom edge of the front bumper. Finding plastic abrasions that existed six renters ago, they levy a **3,000 MAD (€275) bumper repaint fee**.

### 3. The Pre-Printed Damage Matrix (*Barème des Dégâts*)
When a legitimate Moroccan body shop (*tôlerie-peinture*) repaints a scratched door panel on a Dacia Duster, the actual B2B cost to a fleet owner is 500 to 700 MAD (€45–€65). However, budget rental desks force you to sign a pre-printed damage matrix at pickup that assigns arbitrary, astronomical penalties:
*   Scratch > 2 cm on any panel: **2,200 MAD (€200)**
*   Scuffed plastic hubcap (*enjoliveur*): **600 MAD (€55)** (Actual cost at Marjane supermarket: 60 MAD)
*   Windshield micro-pit (*impact pare-brise*): **3,500 MAD (€320)**
*   Interior sand/dust penalty (*frais de nettoyage approfondi*): **500 MAD (€46)**

### 4. The Early Morning Flight Squeeze
If you have a 6:30 AM Ryanair or EasyJet flight out of Marrakech or Fez-Saïss, you arrive at the return lot at 4:30 AM. If the agent fabricates a 4,000 MAD damage claim, they know you have exactly 20 minutes before your boarding gate closes. You do not have time to call the *Police Touristique* or contest the charge; you are forced to sign the deduction slip or risk missing your flight home.

callout.text: During your pickup video inspection in Morocco, always film three non-obvious zones with your smartphone flash on: (1) Underneath the front bumper lip, (2) Inside the trunk under the mat showing the spare tire and jack, and (3) The windshield from inside looking out against the light to reveal micro-chips.

sections.heading: How to Vet and Book a Legitimate Local Moroccan Agency (The 6-Point Protocol)
sections.content:
Shifting from international aggregators to a reputable local Moroccan agency eliminates the middleman commission, aligns the agency's incentives with customer retention rather than desk extraction, and cuts your deposit liability by up to 85%. However, Morocco has over 4,500 registered car rental companies—ranging from elite professional fleets to informal two-car brokers operating out of cafés in Gueliz.

Follow this strict 6-point forensic protocol to verify a local Moroccan rental agency before transferring a single dirham:

1.  **Verify Corporate Legal Identifiers (RC & ICE):** Every legitimate Moroccan agency operates as a registered SARL (Société à Responsabilité Limitée) holding transport authorization from the Ministry of Equipment and Transport. Check their website footer or invoice for their **RC (*Registre de Commerce*)** and their 15-digit **ICE (*Identifiant Commun de l'Entreprise*)**. Never rent from individuals on Facebook Marketplace offering private cars (*voitures particulières*), as private insurance policies are 100% void when the vehicle is rented for profit.
2.  **Enforce the 2024/2025 CNDP ID Card Law:** Under Moroccan National Commission for the Control of Personal Data Protection (**CNDP**) directives, it is **strictly illegal** for a car rental agency to retain your physical passport or Moroccan National ID (CIN) as a security guarantee (*gage*). Nor are they permitted to photocopy your bank card front-and-back (exposing your CVV). Legitimate agencies take a digital scan or photocopy of your passport and driving license, and immediately hand the originals back.
3.  **Demand Pre-Arrival WhatsApp Confirmation of Total Price & Deposit:** Before confirming, message the agency on WhatsApp and get explicit written confirmation of: (a) Exact daily rate in MAD, (b) Exact deposit amount (*caution*) and whether it can be paid in cash or debit card, (c) Whether mileage is unlimited (*kilométrage illimité*), and (d) Whether *Bris de Glace* (glass/tires) is included.
4.  **Audit Fleet Age (Maximum 36 Months):** Due to Morocco's rough secondary road surfaces and heat, never rent a vehicle older than 3 years or with more than 80,000 km on the odometer. Reputable local agencies cycle their Dacia, Renault, and Hyundai fleets every 24 to 30 months.
5.  **Understand the 'Quart-par-Quart' Fuel Rule:** Unlike European full-to-full policies, 90% of Moroccan agencies operate on a *même niveau* (same-to-same) fuel rule—usually handing you the car with 1/4 or 2/8 of a tank. Photograph the dashboard cluster showing both exact mileage and fuel bars before putting the car in gear.
6.  **Insist on the Grey Card (*Carte Grise*) Inspection:** When receiving the vehicle documents at the airport, verify that you have the physical *Attestation d'Assurance* (check expiration date), the *Visite Technique* (if the car is over 5 years old), and the *Carte Grise* (or certified *Autorisation de Circulation* if newly leased). Driving past a *Gendarmerie Royale* checkpoint without valid original or certified registration documents results in an immediate 300 to 700 MAD fine and potential vehicle impoundment (*fourrière*).

callout.text: At ZwinCar, every partner fleet is pre-audited against these exact metrics: guaranteed vehicles under 36 months old, transparent 0 to 5,000 MAD deposits payable via Debit/Credit/Cash, zero hidden airport fees, and direct WhatsApp line before you even board your flight.

faqs.question: Is DiscoverCars or Rentalcars legit in Morocco, or is it a scam?
faqs.answer: DiscoverCars, Rentalcars, and BSP Auto are legitimate international tech brokers, not direct rental agencies. However, their business model in Morocco creates a 'soft scam' environment: by advertising mathematically impossible rates of €6 to €10/day (65–110 MAD/day), they pass you to ultra-low-cost local fulfillment desks that must aggressively extract 2,000 to 4,000 MAD from you at the counter via rejected debit cards, mandatory 300 MAD/day insurance upsells, or fabricated 2cm scratch claims upon return.

faqs.question: Why did the Moroccan car rental desk reject my credit card and force me to buy insurance?
faqs.answer: Moroccan CMI payment terminals require a true 'CREDIT' card (with a credit BIN and often the word CREDIT physically printed on the card) to lock a 15,000 to 25,000 MAD pre-authorization deposit. Most European cards (including French 'Carte Bleue' debit/deferred debit) and all neo-bank cards (Revolut, Wise, N26) read as Debit. Budget desks use this technicality to declare your card invalid for the deposit, forcing you to buy their non-refundable Super CDW insurance at 250–350 MAD (€23–€32) per day.

faqs.question: How much does a reliable car rental actually cost per day in Morocco with no hidden fees?
faqs.answer: In 2026, a transparent, well-maintained rental car from a vetted local Moroccan agency costs between 250 and 320 MAD (€23–€30) per day for a manual compact (Dacia Sandero, Kia Picanto), 330 to 420 MAD (€30–€39) per day for an automatic hatchback (Renault Clio 5, Peugeot 208), and 450 to 650 MAD (€42–€60) per day for an SUV (Dacia Duster, Hyundai Tucson). These realistic rates include comprehensive local insurance and require low deposits (0 to 5,000 MAD).

faqs.question: Can I rent a car in Morocco with a debit card or cash deposit?
faqs.answer: You cannot rent with a debit card or cash if you book through international brokers (Rentalcars, Expedia, DiscoverCars) or major international airport franchises without paying punitive daily waiver fees. However, vetted local Moroccan agencies routinely accept Visa/Mastercard debit cards or cash deposits (in MAD, EUR, GBP, or USD) ranging from 3,000 to 5,000 MAD (€280–€460), which is returned immediately in cash at the airport when you hand back the keys.

faqs.question: Is it legal for a Moroccan car rental agency to keep my passport or ask for a blank cheque?
faqs.answer: No, both practices are strictly illegal in Morocco. Under Moroccan Penal Code Article 544, demanding or issuing a cheque as a security guarantee ('chèque de garantie') is a criminal offense punishable by imprisonment and heavy fines. Similarly, CNDP data protection laws prohibit agencies from confiscating your physical passport or national ID card. Only provide a photocopy/scan of your passport and driving license.

title: Driving in Morocco as a Foreign Tourist in 2026: Traffic Laws, Priority-to-the-Right Roundabouts & Signs
metaDescription: Master driving in Morocco tourist rules for 2026: survive priority-to-the-right roundabouts, decode bilingual road signs, and avoid 400 MAD radar fines.

author.name: Hamza Benjelloun
author.role: Moroccan Road Logistics Expert & Fleet Auditor

summaryDirectAnswer: Driving in Morocco is regulated by Law 52-05 (Code de la Route). Unlike standard European road systems, many urban Moroccan roundabouts enforce strict 'priorité à droite' (priority to the right), requiring vehicles already inside the circle to stop and yield to entering traffic unless an inverted triangle sign ('Cédez le passage') is explicitly posted at the entry. Speed tolerances are strictly zero above a 7 km/h technical margin, with immediate cash fines ranging from 150 MAD to 700 MAD (€15–€70).

sections.heading: The Moroccan Roundabout Paradox: 'Carrefour Giratoire' vs. 'Rond-Point'
sections.content:
The single highest cause of rental car insurance claims in urban hubs like Casablanca, Rabat, and Marrakech is a fundamental misunderstanding of Moroccan roundabout mechanics. Most foreign drivers operate on the assumption that vehicles inside a roundabout always hold the right of way. Under Moroccan Law 52-05, this is legally false in roughly 40% of urban intersections.

Moroccan traffic engineering distinguishes strictly between two circular intersection types:

1. **Le Carrefour Giratoire (Modern Yield-at-Entry Roundabout):** Identified by a dashed white yield line painted across the entry lane and an inverted red-and-white triangle sign (*Cédez le passage*). Here, standard European and UK rules apply: traffic inside the circle has priority, and entering vehicles must yield.
2. **Le Rond-Point Classique (Traditional Priority-to-the-Right Circle):** Identified by the **complete absence** of road markings or yield signs at the entry point. Frequently found around historic medina perimeters, monumental plazas (such as Place Mohammed V in Casablanca or central avenues in Gueliz, Marrakech), and older municipal zones. Under Article 56 of the *Code de la Route*, in the absence of explicit signage, *priorité à droite* (priority to the right) governs the intersection. **You must stop inside the roundabout to let entering cars in.**

### Forensic Comparison of Moroccan Circular Intersections

| Feature | Carrefour Giratoire (Standard) | Rond-Point Classique (Priority Right) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Entry Signage** | Inverted Triangle (*Cédez le passage*) | None (or explicit *Priorité à droite* triangle) |
| **Road Markings** | Thick dashed white line at entry | No entry line; bare asphalt |
| **Who Has Right of Way?** | Vehicles **inside** the circle | Vehicles **entering** from the right |
| **Typical Locations** | National highways (Routes Nationales), rural bypasses, post-2010 suburbs | City centers (Casablanca, Rabat, Fes), monumental squares |
| **Insurance Fault if Hit** | Entering vehicle is 100% at fault | Vehicle already in the circle is 100% at fault |

### How to Audit a Roundabout at 40 km/h
When approaching any circular intersection in Morocco, ignore the geometry of the island and look exclusively at the entry asphalt and the right-hand signpost of the **next** entry branch:
* **Step 1:** Check your own entry for a dashed white line. If absent, assume everyone entering at the next junction has the legal right to cut directly in front of you.
* **Step 2:** As you circulate, look at the backs of the signs facing the drivers waiting to enter at the next spoke. If you see the back of an inverted triangle, you hold priority. If there is no sign pole, cover your brake immediately—local taxis (*Petits Taxis*) will enter without looking at you because the law backs them.

callout.text: In a 'Rond-Point Classique', if you are circulating inside the ring and collide with a vehicle entering from your right, the Constat Amiable (accident report) will assign 100% legal liability to you, voiding standard third-party coverage for your rental vehicle's front-end damage.

sections.heading: Statutory Framework: Law 52-05 (Code de la Route) & Fine Structure
sections.content:
Moroccan road enforcement underwent a structural overhaul with the enactment of **Dahir n° 1-10-07 promulgating Law 52-05**, further updated by **Law 116-14** and enforced digitally by **NARSA** (*Agence Nationale de la Sécurité Routière*). Foreign tourists are subject to the exact same statutory penalties as residents, with one critical operational difference: because foreign licenses cannot be docked Moroccan demerit points (out of the standard 30-point domestic allocation), officers strictly enforce immediate payment of the *Amende Transactionnelle et Forfaitaire* (ATF).

Under the statutory grading system, traffic violations are divided into three tiers. If you pay on the spot (or within 24 hours at a designated *Trésorerie Générale* or via an officer's mobile TPE card terminal), you benefit from a statutory discount of roughly 43%. Do not confuse this discounted on-the-spot rate with a bribe; it is written directly into Article 219 of the Traffic Code.

### 2026 Moroccan Traffic Fine Schedule (ATF Rates)

| Violation Class | Common Offenses Included | Full Statutory Fine | Immediate Payment (Within 24h) | Paid Within 15 Days |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1st Class** | Exceeding speed by 20–30 km/h; crossing a solid white line (*ligne continue*); failing to stop at a *STOP* (*Qif*) sign; driving in the opposite direction; dangerous overtaking. | 700 MAD (€65) | **400 MAD (€37)** | 500 MAD (€46) |
| **2nd Class** | Exceeding speed by <20 km/h; handheld mobile phone use (including touching a mounted screen); failure to wear a seatbelt (front or rear passengers); failure to yield at a roundabout; entering a highway pedestrian zone. | 500 MAD (€46) | **300 MAD (€28)** | 350 MAD (€32) |
| **3rd Class** | Exceeding speed by <10% in urban zones; faulty headlight/brake light bulb; improper urban parking; failure to display vehicle rental dossier when requested. | 300 MAD (€28) | **150 MAD (€14)** | 200 MAD (€18) |

### Critical Legal Thresholds to Memorize
* **Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC):** Essentially **0.00%**. Morocco enforces a strict ban on driving under the influence. The technical legal breathalyzer threshold is 0.20 mg/l of exhaled air (0.40 g/l blood), which triggers an immediate criminal indictment, vehicle impoundment, and a fine between 5,000 and 10,000 MAD (€460–€925). Do not consume even half a glass of wine before driving.
* **Speeding Over 30 km/h:** Exceeding the posted limit by 30 to 50 km/h elevates the offense out of the standard ATF bracket to a **1,400 MAD** fine (discounted to **800 MAD** if paid immediately). Exceeding by 50 km/h or more is a criminal misdemeanor requiring license confiscation and court appearance.
* **Rear Seatbelts:** Since 2018, the *Gendarmerie Royale* actively checks rear passenger seatbelts at highway toll exits. Each unbuckled rear passenger incurs a separate 300 MAD immediate fine.

callout.text: When paying an on-the-spot fine (ATF) in cash, the officer is legally required to issue an official green or white perforated government receipt (Quittance) stamped with the Ministry of Equipment and Water seal. Never hand over cash without receiving this receipt.

sections.heading: Decoding Moroccan Signage: Arabic, Tifinagh, French & Speed Traps
sections.content:
Moroccan road signage follows the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Signs and Signals—meaning shapes and color codes mirror continental Europe (red circles for prohibitions, blue circles for mandatory actions, red triangles for hazards). However, directional and regulatory legends are trilingual, written in **Classical Arabic**, **Amazigh (Tifinagh script)**, and **French**.

While major *Autoroutes* (ADM toll highways) feature clear Latin script well in advance of exits, rural secondary roads (*Routes Régionales* and *Routes Provinciales*) and historic city centers present three major navigational hazards for foreign tourists.

### 1. The 'Qif' (قف) Stop Sign
Older octagonal red STOP signs in rural provinces, the High Atlas, and urban medina perimeters display only the Arabic script **قف** (*Qif*). Regardless of whether the Latin letters 'STOP' appear, the red octagon mandates a **complete mechanical halt** where the vehicle's wheels stop rotating for a full two seconds behind the white line. Rolling through a *Qif* sign at 3 km/h is one of the top revenue generators for municipal police (*Sûreté Nationale*), triggering a Class 1 fine of 400 MAD.

### 2. The Descending Speed Cascade (100 → 80 → 60 → 40)
When driving on National Routes (such as the N8 between Marrakech and Beni Mellal, or the N9 over Tizi n'Tichka), entering any rural commune or approaching a Gendarmerie checkpoint triggers a rapid, aggressive speed step-down. Within 400 meters, signs will drop from 100 km/h to 80, then 60, and finally 40 or 20 km/h at the checkpoint barrier.
* **The Trap:** Foreign drivers typically coast gently by lifting off the accelerator, still traveling at 72 km/h as they pass the 60 km/h sign. Gendarmerie officers position portable tripod laser guns (TruCAM II) **30 meters behind the 60 km/h sign**. You must actively brake *before* passing the sign plane.

### 3. Missing 'End of Restriction' Signs
On secondary roads, roadworks or hazard zones frequently post a temporary 40 km/h limit sign, but the crew never installs the white-and-black diagonal *Fin de limitation* (End of speed limit) sign. Legally, under Moroccan law, a speed restriction placed before a specific hazard or intersection resets **after you clear that intersection**. However, if the sign simply stands on an open stretch of rural road, maintain the reduced speed for at least 1.5 kilometers or until the next major crossroads before resuming 80 or 100 km/h.

### Essential Road Terminology Glossary
* **Ralentir / خفف السرعة:** Slow down immediately (indicates an imminent police checkpoint, radar, or sharp hairpin).
* **Chaussée Déformée:** Deformed/sunken tarmac. Slow down to 50 km/h; hitting a subsided culvert at 90 km/h in a compact hatchback will rupture your oil pan.
* **Radier Submersible:** Floodable concrete river crossing (common in the Draa and Dades valleys). Never cross if water obscures the concrete edges.
* **Priorité à Droite:** Yield to all vehicles entering from right-hand side streets.

callout.text: Watch oncoming local drivers—especially Grand Taxis (old Mercedes sedans or Dacia Lodgys). Two sharp flashes of their high beams mean a mobile Gendarmerie radar tripod is hidden within the next 800 meters.

sections.heading: Police Checkpoints ('Barrages'), Mobile Radars & Mandatory Vehicle Documents
sections.content:
Foreign drivers are frequently intimidated by the high density of uniformed checkpoints across Morocco. In reality, checkpoints are routine administrative filters, and tourists are waved through 90% of the time—provided you follow the strict approach protocol.

### Who Controls Which Roads?
1. **DGSN (Sûreté Nationale - Police):** Wear dark blue or black uniforms with white caps. They have jurisdiction exclusively **inside urban municipal boundaries**.
2. **Gendarmerie Royale:** Wear pearl-grey/military green uniforms with peaked caps and drive white/grey SUVs or motorcycles. They enforce the law on **all rural roads, national highways, and Autoroute toll plazas**. They operate the vast majority of portable laser speed guns.

### The 3-Step Checkpoint ('Barrage') Protocol
Every fixed checkpoint at city entrances/exits features a series of staggered metal chicane barriers and a red octagonal sign reading **HALTE POLICE** or **HALTE GENDARMERIE**.
1. **Decelerate Early:** Step down through the 60 → 40 → 20 km/h signs strictly.
2. **Stop at the 'Halte' Sign:** Even if no officer is standing in the lane, come to a near-halt (under 10 km/h) or complete stop at the *Halte* sign, lower your sunglasses, turn down the radio, and roll down the driver's window halfway.
3. **Wait for the Hand Wave:** Maintain eye contact with the officer observing from the roadside booth or shade. Only accelerate once they give the subtle flick of the wrist or forward finger wave. **Never accelerate through a checkpoint without visual clearance.**

### The 6 Mandatory Documents You Must Audit Before Leaving the Rental Desk
If stopped for a routine document check (*Contrôle Routier*), missing paperwork results in a 300 MAD fine—and the driver is legally held liable, even if the rental agency forgot to put the folder in the glovebox. Before turning the ignition key at pickup, verify the physical presence of:
1. **Contrat de Location (Rental Agreement):** Must list every authorized driver by passport and license number.
2. **Carte Grise (Vehicle Registration):** Either the biometric plastic card or a certified stamped copy (*Récépissé*) valid for rental fleets.
3. **Attestation d'Assurance:** The physical yellow or green insurance certificate with valid dates covering your entire trip.
4. **Vignette (TSAVA):** Annual road tax receipt.
5. **Visite Technique:** Technical inspection certificate (mandatory if the rental vehicle is over 5 years old—though ZwinCar fleet audits ensure vehicles are under 36 months).
6. **Vierge Constat Amiable:** A blank duplicate carbon-copy European-style accident report form, plus a safety triangle and high-visibility vest (*Gilet Jaune*) stored in the cabin or trunk.

callout.text: Fixed NARSA automated radar cabins in 2026 monitor BOTH directions of traffic simultaneously and capture rear license plates. Do not accelerate immediately after passing a grey radar box; wait until you are at least 150 meters past it.

sections.heading: The Unwritten Street Code: Navigating Urban Chaos & Rural Night Hazards
sections.content:
Understanding the statutory *Code de la Route* is only half the equation; surviving unscathed requires adapting to Morocco's informal kinetic street dynamics. Local driving is neither aggressive nor malicious—it is **fluid and nose-first**. Drivers expect you to react exclusively to what is inside your 180-degree forward windshield cone.

### Urban Survival: Casablanca, Marrakech & Fes
* **The Scooter Swarm (Marrakech & Casa):** In Marrakech, 50cc and 110cc mopeds (*C90s*) ignore lane markings entirely, filtering simultaneously on both your left and right flanks. **Rule:** Never make a sudden lateral steering correction to dodge a pothole inside a city without checking both wing mirrors. Hold a predictable, dead-straight line in your lane; the scooters will flow around you like water around a rock.
* **Petits Taxis (Urban Taxis):** Painted red in Casablanca/Fes, ochre in Marrakech, and blue in Rabat. They are legally permitted to stop anywhere on a boulevard to pick up a hailing passenger. Never tailgate a Petit Taxi in the right-hand lane; leave a minimum 2-car buffer, as they will slam their brakes without engaging a turn signal the instant a pedestrian raises a hand on the sidewalk.
* **Lane Splitting (2 Lanes Become 4):** Wide urban avenues frequently lose their painted lane lines. Keep your nose slightly offset from the car ahead so you cannot be boxed in, and yield peacefully if another car inserts its front bumper 30 centimeters ahead of yours.

### Rural & Mountain Survival: The Atlas & Pre-Sahara
* **Narrow Tarmac Shoulders (*Pistes Mixtes*):** Secondary roads in the south (e.g., around Ouarzazate, Zagora, or Chefchaouen backroads) sometimes feature a single central strip of asphalt barely 4 meters wide with rough gravel drops (*accotements*) on either side. When an oncoming truck or bus approaches, decelerate to 40 km/h, place your **right two wheels smoothly onto the gravel shoulder**, let the heavy vehicle pass, and steer gently back onto the tarmac without jerking the wheel (which causes gravel spin-outs).
* **Triporteurs & Unlit Carts:** Three-wheeled cargo motorcycles (*Triporteurs*) and donkey carts operate heavily between rural *souks* (markets). They struggle up gradients at 15 km/h and almost never have functioning rear tail lights. This is the primary reason why **driving outside toll highways after sunset is strongly discouraged**. An unlit dark-grey Triporteur or stray dromedary is invisible against asphalt until it is 25 meters inside your low-beam cone.

callout.text: Select the right transmission for your environment: if your itinerary includes more than 48 hours inside Casablanca, Rabat, or Marrakech, book an automatic hatchback like the Renault Clio 5 Auto or Peugeot 208 PureTech to eliminate clutch fatigue in stop-and-go roundabout queues. For rural shoulder step-offs and Atlas climbs, the raised 162mm ground clearance of a Dacia Sandero Stepway protects your undercarriage.

faqs.question: Do I need an International Driving Permit (IDP) to rent and drive a car in Morocco in 2026?
faqs.answer: No, if your domestic driver's license is printed in the Latin alphabet (such as licenses from the EU, UK, USA, Canada, or Australia) and you are staying as a tourist for less than one year (with a valid passport entry stamp under 90 days). Under the 1968 Vienna Convention, your original physical plastic license is 100% legally valid at all police and Gendarmerie checkpoints. An IDP (1949 or 1968 convention) is only mandatory if your license is printed exclusively in non-Latin script (e.g., Chinese, Cyrillic, Japanese, or Greek). Digital licenses on smartphone apps are strictly rejected by Moroccan police.

faqs.question: What is the speed limit tolerance on Moroccan radars?
faqs.answer: Moroccan fixed and mobile laser radars apply a strict 10% technical margin capped at a maximum of 7 km/h. Specifically: in a 60 km/h urban zone, you will be flashed at 67 km/h; in an 80 km/h zone, at 88 km/h; in a 100 km/h national route zone, at 108 km/h; and on a 120 km/h Autoroute, you are penalized starting at 128 km/h. Exceeding the threshold by even 1 km/h over the margin triggers an automatic Class 2 fine of 500 MAD (reduced to 300 MAD if paid immediately).

faqs.question: What happens if I get flashed by an automated fixed camera in a rental car?
faqs.answer: When a fixed NARSA radar flashes your rental vehicle, the digital citation is routed to the registered fleet owner (the rental agency) within 48 to 72 hours via the Infractions Routières portal. Under Moroccan Law 116-14, the agency is legally required to submit the identity and passport details of the renter listed on the contract for that timestamp. The statutory fine is either settled via your security deposit upon vehicle return (usually with a small administrative processing fee) or sent to your address. You can also ask your agency to check the NARSA portal before you fly home so you can pay the discounted rate (300 or 400 MAD) instead of the full 500 or 700 MAD rate.

faqs.question: Can I turn right on a red light in Morocco?
faqs.answer: No. Turning right on a solid red traffic light is strictly illegal in Morocco and is treated as running a red light (a Class 1 violation carrying an immediate 400 MAD fine). The only exception is when the intersection features a dedicated right-turn slip lane separated by a physical concrete island, OR when a separate flashing yellow arrow signal is illuminated specifically for the right-hand lane. Even with a flashing yellow arrow, you must yield to pedestrians crossing the intersection.

faqs.question: What is the exact procedure if I have a minor fender-bender in a Moroccan roundabout?
faqs.answer: Do not move the vehicles if there is a dispute over fault, especially inside a 'Rond-Point Classique' where lane positioning proves who held priority. Switch on your hazard lights, take immediate wide-angle photos of both cars showing the road markings (or lack thereof) and license plates, and fill out the carbon-copy Constat Amiable found in your glovebox. If the other driver refuses to sign or demands cash on the spot, refuse politely, stay inside or next to your vehicle, call your rental agency's 24/7 assistance number, and dial 19 (inside cities for Police) or 177 (outside cities for Gendarmerie Royale) so an officer can draw an official croquis (accident sketch).

title: Morocco Police Checkpoints Guide: Gendarmerie Royale vs Sûreté Nationale, Stop Signs & Inspection Protocol
metaDescription: Navigate Morocco police checkpoints safely. Learn the Gendarmerie Royale vs DGSN protocols, Stop vs Ralentir rules, exact fine amounts in MAD, and legal rights.

author.name: Hamza Benjelloun
author.role: Moroccan Road Logistics Expert & Fleet Auditor

summaryDirectAnswer: Moroccan road checkpoints are operated by two bodies: the Sûreté Nationale (DGSN) at urban perimeters and the military Gendarmerie Royale on rural highways. Drivers must reduce speed from 60 km/h to 20 km/h at chicanes. At 'Halte Police/Gendarmerie' signs, you must achieve a complete, zero-rotation wheel stop and wait for an officer's explicit wave before proceeding. Tourists are rarely inspected if speed protocols are obeyed. Under Law 52-05, legitimate on-the-spot fines require an official stamped receipt (Quittance) ranging from 150 to 700 MAD.

sections.heading: Jurisdictional Anatomy: Sûreté Nationale (DGSN) vs. Gendarmerie Royale
sections.content:
Understanding who is stopping you on Moroccan roads requires distinguishing between two entirely separate ministries and command chains. When exiting major hubs like Marrakech, Agadir, or Tangier, the transition from urban boulevards to national highways marks a hard jurisdictional boundary.

**1. Direction Générale de la Sûreté Nationale (DGSN - Police):**
Operating under the Ministry of the Interior, the DGSN controls all municipal perimeters, urban ring roads, and city entry/exit points (*Barrages Judiciaires*). You will identify them by their dark blue or black tactical uniforms, white utility vehicles (often Dacia Dokkers, Renault Trafics, or Skoda Octavias) with blue and red livery, and white traffic helmets for motorcycle units. Their primary mandate at city gates is national security, verifying vehicle registration anomalies, and screening commercial transport.

**2. La Gendarmerie Royale:**
Once you pass the municipal boundary sign (marked by a red horizontal line through the city name), you enter the jurisdiction of the Gendarmerie Royale, an branch of the Royal Moroccan Armed Forces reporting to the Administration of National Defense. Gendarmes wear distinctive pearl-grey uniforms, white Sam Browne belts, and peaked caps (or blue berets). Their fleet consists of pearl-grey or dark-blue SUVs (Dacia Duster 4x4, Toyota Prado, Volkswagen Touareg) and BMW R1250RT motorcycles. The Gendarmerie controls all *Routes Nationales* (RN), *Routes Régionales* (RR), rural tracks, and the entire *Autoroutes du Maroc* (ADM) toll network.

| Feature | Sûreté Nationale (DGSN) | Gendarmerie Royale |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Jurisdiction** | Urban areas, city limits, municipal gateways | Rural highways (RN/RR), mountain passes, ADM Tollways |
| **Uniform Color** | Dark Navy Blue / Black Tactical | Pearl Grey with White Accents |
| **Primary Focus** | Security screening, urban traffic violations, stolen vehicles | Speed enforcement (TruCAM), highway code compliance, rural security |
| **Authority Type** | Civilian Police Force (Ministry of Interior) | Military Force (National Defense) |
| **Tourist Interaction** | Extremely brief; usually waved through at city gates | Strict adherence to highway code; zero tolerance for speeding or lane violations |

Many foreign drivers operate under the outdated belief that Moroccan roadblocks exist to harass tourists. In reality, since the modernization of the DGSN and Gendarmerie directives between 2018 and 2025, officers operate under strict orders to facilitate tourist transit. Over 90% of rental vehicles driven by foreigners are waved through fixed security checkpoints without document inspection—**provided the driver executes the approach protocol correctly.**

callout.text: How do officers know you are driving a rental car from 200 meters away? While Moroccan license plates look uniform, fleet vehicles carry specific municipal registration patterns and subtle windshield vignettes. Furthermore, Gendarmes instantly recognize current-year fleet trims (like a base-spec Renault Clio 5 or Dacia Duster) occupied by non-local drivers.

sections.heading: The Visual Choreography of a 'Barrage': Ralentir vs. Halte Protocol
sections.content:
The vast majority of traffic fines issued to tourists at Moroccan checkpoints do not happen because of pre-existing infractions; they occur **inside the checkpoint zone itself** due to a failure to read the sign sequence. Fixed checkpoints (*Barrages Fixes*) at city entrances and provincial borders follow a rigid spatial layout governed by the Moroccan Highway Code.

### The 4-Stage Approach Sequence

1. **Stage 1: The De-escalation Zone (200m to 100m out):**
   You will see sequential temporary signs on the right shoulder Stepping down the speed limit: **80 km/h -> 60 km/h -> 40 km/h**. You must actively brake, not merely coast. Gendarmes frequently position an optical laser unit *inside* the checkpoint tent to measure your approach speed inside the 60 km/h funnel.
2. **Stage 2: The Chicane & Spike Strip (50m out):**
   The road narrows into a single lane flanked by red-and-white metal barriers and a heavy steel spike strip (*herse*) laid across the asphalt. The speed limit here drops to **20 km/h**. Cross the metal housing of the spike strip at a crawl (10–15 km/h) in first or second gear to avoid damaging rental tires.
3. **Stage 3: The 'Ralentir' vs. 'Halte' Decision Point:**
   At the center of the roadblock stands a portable tripod sign. You must read the exact wording:
   * **RALENTIR (Slow Down):** Keep the vehicle moving at walking pace (10 km/h). Maintain eye contact with the primary officer standing on the shoulder.
   * **HALTE POLICE / قف الدرك الملكي (Stop Gendarmerie):** You must bring the vehicle to a **complete mechanical stop** two meters before the sign. Your wheels must achieve zero rotation for at least two full seconds.
4. **Stage 4: Nighttime Protocol & Visual Clearance:**
   If approaching a checkpoint between dusk and dawn, you must **switch off your dipped headlights (feux de croisement) and keep only your position/parking lights (feux de position) on**, while turning **ON your interior cabin dome light**. This prevents blinding the officers and allows them to see the occupants' hands and faces immediately.

Never accelerate out of a checkpoint until the officer gives you a clear physical gesture—either a circular forward wave of the hand during the day, or a horizontal sweep of a green/white flashlight wand at night. Executing a 'California rolling stop' at a *Halte* sign is legally classified under Moroccan law as running a red light/stop sign, triggering an immediate 700 MAD fine.

callout.text: Never photograph, film, or leave a dashboard camera (Dashcam) actively pointed at officers during a checkpoint approach. Recording military or police installations (including mobile Gendarmerie roadblocks) is a severe national security offense in Morocco. If you use a dashcam, unplug it and dismount it before entering Morocco.

sections.heading: The Document Pouch Audit: What Officers Actually Inspect
sections.content:
When an officer raises their palm vertically and points to the dirt shoulder, you are being pulled over for a routine administrative audit (*Contrôle Routier*). Turn on your right indicator, pull completely off the asphalt, shift into park/neutral, engage the handbrake, and lower your driver-side window fully. Do not exit the vehicle unless instructed.

The greeting sets the tone: a polite *"Salam Alaykoum, Mon Commandant"* (or simply *"Bonjour Monsieur"*) demonstrates cultural competence. The officer will request *"Les papiers du véhicule"* (vehicle documents). Every legitimate Moroccan rental agency provides a plastic pouch in the glovebox. Before leaving the rental depot in Marrakech, Ouarzazate, or Tangier, you must verify that this pouch contains five specific physical documents:

1. **Certificat d'Immatriculation (Carte Grise):** Often a plasticized biometric card or an official notarized copy bearing the stamp *"Copie Certifiée Conforme"*, proving the car's registration.
2. **Attestation d'Assurance:** The physical green or yellow paper insurance certificate. Check the expiration date to ensure it covers your entire trip duration.
3. **Contrat de Location (Rental Agreement):** The carbon-copy sheet linking your name and passport number to the vehicle's chassis. **Crucial:** If a second person is driving, their full name and driving license number must be explicitly written on this contract; otherwise, the insurance is void and the police will immobilize the vehicle.
4. **Vignette Fiscal (TSAVA):** Proof of annual road tax payment (usually a digital receipt printed on A4 paper).
5. **Autorisation de Circulation (For new cars):** If your rental car has temporary plates ending in **"WW"** (meaning it is brand new), it must have a valid temporary circulation permit.

Along with the vehicle pouch, hand over your **Physical National Driving License** and your **Passport** (turned to the page showing your Moroccan border entry stamp/number). Under the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic, drivers holding valid national licenses in the Latin alphabet (EU, UK, US, Canada, Australia) do not legally require an International Driving Permit (IDP) for stays under 90 days, though carrying one prevents confusion if your license lacks a clear issue/expiry format.

callout.text: Perform a 60-second 'Glovebox Audit' before driving out of your rental agency. If the insurance certificate expires mid-trip, or if the technical inspection certificate (Visite Technique—mandatory for rental cars over 1 year old) is missing, you—the driver—will be fined 300 MAD at the first Gendarmerie checkpoint.

sections.heading: Mobile Speed Traps, LTI TruCAM Lasers & Law 52-05 Fines
sections.content:
While fixed checkpoints at city gates focus on security and paperwork, mobile Gendarmerie units positioned along national routes (such as the N9 over the Tizi n'Tichka pass to Ouarzazate, or the N1 coastal road south of Agadir) are exclusively focused on traffic enforcement under **Law 52-05 (Code de la Route)**, as amended by Law 116-14.

### How Mobile Traps Operate
Unlike Europe, where speed cameras are painted bright yellow, Moroccan Gendarmerie mobile traps are camouflaged. An officer sits in the shade of an olive tree, behind a bridge abutment, or inside a civilian-looking vehicle equipped with an **LTI 20/20 TruCAM II** laser binocular. This device captures high-definition video and still photos of your license plate, your speed, and the **driver's face through the windshield** from up to 1,200 meters away. About 400 to 800 meters further down the road, a second team of Gendarmes stands ready to intercept the flagged vehicle.

### The 10% Tolerance Rule
Moroccan radar enforcement applies a strict **10% margin of error** (up to a maximum of 7 km/h) on speed limits:
* In a **60 km/h** zone: You are flashed/stopped at **67 km/h**.
* In an **80 km/h** zone: You are flashed/stopped at **88 km/h**.
* In a **100 km/h** zone: You are flashed/stopped at **107 km/h**.
* In a **120 km/h** zone (Autoroute): You are flashed/stopped at **128 km/h**.

### Official Fine Tiers (Amendes Transactionnelles et Forfaitaires - ATF)
Under Law 116-14, if you pay your fine on the spot (in cash, Dirhams only) or within 24 hours, you benefit from a statutory discount:

| Class | Typical Infractions | Base Fine (MAD) | Immediate Cash Payment (MAD / ~EUR) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1st Class** | Speeding by 20 to 30 km/h; Crossing a solid white line (*Ligne continue*); Failing to stop at a *Halte* sign; Dangerous overtaking. | 700 MAD | **400 MAD (~37 €)** |
| **2nd Class** | Speeding by less than 20 km/h; Using a handheld phone while driving; Front OR rear passenger not wearing a seatbelt; Driving without headlights at night. | 500 MAD | **300 MAD (~28 €)** |
| **3rd Class** | Minor lighting defect; Failure to display '90' sticker (if applicable); Expired minor local permit. | 300 MAD | **150 MAD (~14 €)** |

*Note: Exceeding the speed limit by 30 to 50 km/h incurs a steeper tier, while exceeding by 50 km/h or more is a criminal offense resulting in immediate license confiscation and a court summons.*

callout.text: The Rear Seatbelt Trap: Under Moroccan law, seatbelts are mandatory for ALL occupants, including those in the back seat, when driving on rural highways (hors agglomération). Gendarmes routinely look into the rear windows as you roll through a 20 km/h checkpoint. Unbelted rear passengers trigger an immediate 300 MAD fine.

sections.heading: The Anti-Corruption Shift: Handling Fines, Receipts & Disputes
sections.content:
A persistent myth propagated by outdated travel blogs is that Moroccan police routinely solicit bribes (*bakchich*) of 50 to 100 MAD from foreign tourists, and that you should carry a 'dummy wallet' to negotiate them down. **Applying this advice in 2026 is the fastest way to get arrested for active corruption of a public official.**

Following aggressive anti-corruption campaigns led by the DGSN and the Gendarmerie High Command—backed by royal directives and a dedicated citizen anti-bribery hotline—officers are acutely aware that tourists carry smartphones and that internal affairs units conduct undercover stings. Today's officers are professional, procedural, and bound by strict audit trails.

### The Legitimate Payment Protocol
If you have committed a genuine infraction (e.g., forgetting your seatbelt or doing 72 km/h in a 60 km/h transition zone), follow this exact protocol:
1. **Request Visual Proof (For Radar/Laser):** If stopped for speeding or crossing a solid line by a remote observer, you have the legal right to politely ask to see the photo/video on the TruCAM unit: *"Est-ce que je peux voir la photo sur le radar, s'il vous plaît ?"* Note that sometimes the camera operator is 800m back and communicates via radio; in this case, the intercepting officer will show you the radio log bearing your license plate and exact speed.
2. **Pay the Exact discounted ATF Amount in Cash:** Keep at least 400 MAD in cash in your vehicle at all times. Mobile POS credit card terminals exist on major tollways, but rural checkpoints rely entirely on cash in Moroccan Dirhams.
3. **Demand the Official Receipt (La Quittance):** When you pay a 150, 300, or 400 MAD fine, the officer **must** write out an official carbon-copy receipt torn from a numbered government booklet (*Carnet à souches*). Verify that the amount written matches what you paid, and keep this paper in your rental pouch.

### How to Handle an Ambiguous or Disputed Stop
In the rare event an officer claims an infraction you are 100% certain you did not commit (e.g., claiming you ran a stop sign when you clearly halted) and stalls without taking out the official receipt booklet:
* **Remain calm, polite, and unhurried.** Never raise your voice or insult the uniform (*Outrage à agent* is a serious felony).
* **Insist on the official process:** State calmly: *"Monsieur l'agent, je respecte la loi. Si j'ai commis une infraction, je paie l'amende officielle avec la quittance réglementaire."* (Officer, I respect the law. If I committed an infraction, I will pay the official fine with the regulatory receipt.)
* **If you refuse to pay on the spot:** By law, if you contest a fine and refuse immediate payment, the officer will draft a *Procès-Verbal* (PV) and confiscate your physical driving license in exchange for a temporary driving permit valid for 30 days, requiring you to pay at a local treasury (*Perception*) or contest it in court. Unless the accusation is outrageous, paying the 300/400 MAD discounted fine against an official receipt is always the most pragmatic logistical choice.

callout.text: Never offer money without requesting a receipt, and never slip folded banknotes inside your passport or vehicle registration pouch. An officer will treat this as an attempted bribe (Tentative de corruption) under Article 248 of the Moroccan Penal Code.

sections.heading: Southern & Desert Corridors: Military Checkpoints and 'Fiches'
sections.content:
If your itinerary takes you into the deep south—specifically beyond **Guelmim, Tan-Tan, Tarfaya, Laâyoune, or Dakhla**, or along the Algerian border tracks near **Merzouga, Zagora, and Tata**—the nature of checkpoints shifts from traffic enforcement to territorial security.

In these zones, alongside the Gendarmerie Royale, you will encounter checkpoints manned by the **Forces Auxiliaires (Makhzen)** and the **Forces Armées Royales (FAR)**. Here, the inspection is never about your tire tread or speed; it is a strict census of foreign movements to ensure traveler safety in remote desert sectors.

### The 'Fiche de Renseignements' Strategy
At every major town entrance south of Guelmim, an officer will ask for your passport and rental contract, walk into a guardhouse, and manually transcribe your details into a large ledger. This takes 5 to 10 minutes per checkpoint. 

Experienced Sahara drivers bypass this delay by preparing **15 to 20 printed 'Fiches de Police'** before departing Agadir or Marrakech. On a standard A4 page (cut into halves or quarters), print the following information clearly in French for each passenger, plus a photocopy of your passport photo page and entry stamp:
* **Nom et Prénom** (Last & First Name)
* **Nationalité** (Nationality)
* **Date et Lieu de Naissance** (Date & Place of Birth)
* **Numéro de Passeport & Date de Délivrance/Expiration**
* **Numéro d'Entrée au Maroc** (The 6-to-8 digit alphanumeric code stamped in your passport by border police upon arrival, e.g., *A123456*)
* **Profession** (Occupation)
* **Provenance et Destination** (e.g., *Agadir -> Dakhla*)
* **Marque du Véhicule et Immatriculation** (e.g., *Toyota Prado - 12345-A-26*)
* **Numéro de Téléphone Marocain** (Local SIM number)

When you stop at a southern checkpoint, hand the officer your physical passport along with one printed *Fiche*. The officer will verify your face, thank you warmly for saving them ten minutes of handwriting, and wave you through in under 30 seconds.

callout.text: When asked for your 'Profession' at a southern checkpoint or on a printed Fiche, avoid listing 'Journalist', 'Photographer', 'Videographer', 'Drone Operator', or 'Military/Defense'. These professions trigger mandatory secondary clearance protocols with regional authorities. Use neutral terms like 'Consultant', 'Teacher' (Enseignant), 'Engineer' (Ingénieur), or 'Manager'.

faqs.question: Can Moroccan police confiscate my foreign driving license at a checkpoint?
faqs.answer: Only if you commit a severe infraction (like speeding by more than 30 km/h over the limit) OR if you refuse to pay an on-the-spot fine (ATF) and lack the cash to settle it immediately. In that scenario, the officer confiscates your physical license and issues a paper receipt (Récépissé) that serves as a temporary driving permit within Morocco until you pay the fine at a local tax office (Perception) or treasury to retrieve your card.

faqs.question: What should I do if I get flashed by an automated fixed speed camera in a rental car?
faqs.answer: Do not panic; fixed automated radars are not linked in real-time to police checkpoints down the road. The fine (300 to 700 MAD) is mailed to the registered owner of the vehicle—your rental car agency—usually 2 to 4 weeks later. The agency is legally required to submit the rental contract naming you as the driver to the Ministry of Transport, or they will notify you and deduct the administrative fee/fine from your security deposit.

faqs.question: Do I have to stop at every police checkpoint in Morocco if there is no officer standing in the road?
faqs.answer: You must always obey the signage regardless of whether you see an officer. If the sign in the middle of the lane says 'HALTE' (Stop), you must come to a complete mechanical stop for 2 seconds and look toward the guard booth or patrol car for a wave before proceeding. If the sign says 'RALENTIR' (Slow Down) and no officer steps out, roll through at 15-20 km/h without stopping.

faqs.question: Are radar detector apps like Waze legal to use in Morocco?
faqs.answer: Yes, using GPS navigation apps like Waze or Google Maps is completely legal and widely used by Moroccan drivers to spot fixed radars and mobile Gendarmerie checkpoints, provided your phone is mounted in a hands-free dashboard holder. Touching or holding a smartphone in your hand while the engine is running on a public road is a 2nd-class offense carrying an immediate 300 MAD cash fine. Physical hardware radar detectors, however, are strictly illegal.

faqs.question: Why did the Gendarmerie stop me when entering a roundabout?
faqs.answer: In Morocco, roundabout priority rules vary depending on signage. While modern urban roundabouts give priority to vehicles already inside the circle (Cédez le passage), many large rural roundabouts near highway checkpoints give priority to traffic entering from the right—OR they feature a hard 'STOP' line right inside the roundabout circulation lane. Always look at the road markings and triangular signs before entering any Moroccan roundabout.

title: Speed Cameras & Mobile Radars in Morocco: Speed Limits, The 400 MAD Fine & Demanding an Official Receipt
metaDescription: Complete legal audit of Morocco's speed limits, 150 MAD vs 400 MAD fines, mobile radar margins, and how to demand an official receipt (quittance).

author.name: Hamza Benjelloun
author.role: Moroccan Road Logistics Expert & Fleet Auditor

summaryDirectAnswer: Under Moroccan Law 116-14 (amending Law 52-05), speeding fines are strictly tiered by excess speed and offer a 50% immediate cash settlement discount (Amende Transactionnelle et Forfaitaire - ATF). Exceeding the limit by under 20 km/h costs 150 MAD (€14) on the spot; 20 to 30 km/h over costs 300 MAD (€28); 30 to 50 km/h over costs 400 MAD (€37). Radars apply a 10% technical margin (max 7 km/h). Always demand a stamped official receipt (quittance) for any roadside cash payment.

sections.heading: The Forensic Reality of Moroccan Speed Limits & The 7 km/h Tolerance Margin
sections.content:
Many foreign drivers enter Morocco assuming enforcement is informal or technologically outdated. In reality, the National Road Safety Agency (NARSA) operates one of the highest-density radar networks in North Africa, backed by the Royal Gendarmerie (outside urban perimeters) and the DGSN National Police (inside municipal boundaries). Understanding the exact mathematical thresholds of the Moroccan Highway Code (Law 52-05, amended by Law 116-14) is the only way to protect your budget and driving privileges.

Standard statutory speed limits in Morocco are segmented into three primary zones:
* **Urban Areas (Agglomérations):** Strictly **60 km/h**, swiftly dropping to **40 km/h** near schools, administrative zones, and coastal boulevards (such as the Casablanca Corniche or Tangier's Avenue Mohammed VI).
* **National & Regional Roads (Routes Nationales):** Capped at **100 km/h**. However, these routes feature frequent, abrupt de-escalation zones (80 km/h down to 60 km/h) whenever passing through rural *douars* (villages) or approaching a Gendarmerie checkpoint (*Barrage Judiciaire*).
* **Autoroutes du Maroc (ADM Highways):** Capped at **120 km/h**, dropping to **100 km/h** or **80 km/h** approaching toll plazas (*Gares de Péage*) and mountainous gradients like the Marrakech–Agadir Argana corridor.

Crucially, Article 184 and its implementing decrees mandate a **technical margin of error (marge de tolérance) of 10%, strictly capped at a maximum of 7 km/h** for both fixed automated radars and mobile handheld laser binoculars (*jumelles*). This is where tourist assumptions fail: a 10% margin on a 120 km/h highway does *not* allow you to drive at 132 km/h. Because the cap is hard-coded at 7 km/h, your absolute trigger speed on the highway is **128 km/h**. At 128 km/h, the radar retains a legal speed of 121 km/h, triggering an immediate Class 3 citation.

| Road Type | Statutory Limit | Technical Tolerance | Max Safe Speed | Radar Trigger Speed |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Urban / Village Transition** | 40 km/h | 4 km/h (10%) | 44 km/h | **45 km/h** |
| **Standard Urban Zone** | 60 km/h | 6 km/h (10%) | 66 km/h | **67 km/h** |
| **Rural Transition / Ring Road** | 80 km/h | 7 km/h (Capped) | 87 km/h | **88 km/h** |
| **National Road (Route Nationale)** | 100 km/h | 7 km/h (Capped) | 107 km/h | **108 km/h** |
| **ADM Toll Highway (Autoroute)** | 120 km/h | 7 km/h (Capped) | 127 km/h | **128 km/h** |

When piloting a highway cruiser like a [Hyundai Tucson Auto](/vehicles/hyundai-tucson-auto) or a [Renault Clio 5 Auto](/vehicles/renault-clio-5-auto), engage your speed limiter (*limiteur de vitesse*)—not just cruise control—at 124 km/h on highways and 62 km/h in cities to eliminate gravitational creep on downhill grades.

callout.text: Downhill grades on the A3 (Casablanca-Rabat) and A2 (Fes-Oujda) are primary placements for mobile laser units. Cruise control often allows a vehicle to coast 3 to 5 km/h above set speed on steep descents—use the active speed limiter function instead.

sections.heading: Deconstructing the '400 MAD Fine' Myth: Statutory Tiers & The 50% Immediate Discount
sections.content:
Travel forums are rife with stories of the infamous "400 Dirham fine" in Morocco, leading tourists to believe 400 MAD (€37) is either a flat-rate arbitrary penalty or a standardized roadside bribe. Both beliefs are factually incorrect. Under Law 116-14, enacted to curb roadside disputes and incentivize immediate clearing of dockets, Morocco introduced a tiered **Amende Transactionnelle et Forfaitaire (ATF)** system with an automatic abatement (discount) for prompt payment.

If you pay a traffic violation **immediately on the spot (sur-le-champ)** or within 24 hours at a designated treasury office, the base statutory fine is legally reduced by roughly **43% to 50%**. If you pay within 15 days, the reduction is roughly 28% to 33%. After 15 days, the full base fine applies, and after 30 days without payment, the case is transferred to the King's Prosecutor (*Procureur du Roi*). 

The reason "400 MAD" echoes across every travel blog is because it is the exact **discounted on-the-spot rate for a First-Class infraction (700 MAD base fine)**—which covers speeding between 30 and 50 km/h over the limit, crossing a solid white line, failing to stop at a STOP sign, or using a handheld phone while driving.

Here is the exact forensic breakdown of Moroccan speeding and traffic fines under Law 116-14:

| Infraction Class & Speed Excess | Base Fine (16–30 Days) | Paid Within 15 Days | Paid Immediately (Same Day) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Class 3:** Speeding **< 20 km/h** over limit (after margin), no seatbelt, helmet fault | 300 MAD (€28) | 200 MAD (€18.50) | **150 MAD (€14)** |
| **Class 2:** Speeding **20 to < 30 km/h** over limit, driving in breakdown lane | 500 MAD (€46) | 350 MAD (€32.50) | **300 MAD (€28)** |
| **Class 1:** Speeding **30 to < 50 km/h** over limit, red light, STOP sign, solid line, phone in hand | 700 MAD (€65) | 500 MAD (€46) | **400 MAD (€37)** |
| **Délit (Criminal Offense):** Speeding **≥ 50 km/h** over limit | **4,000 to 8,000 MAD** | *No Discount* | *Immediate License Seizure & Court* |

Understanding this table shifts your entire roadside negotiation dynamic. If a Gendarme clocks you at 75 km/h in a 60 km/h zone, your retained speed after the 6 km/h tolerance is 69 km/h (+9 km/h over). That is a **Class 3 infraction**, meaning your immediate legal fine is **150 MAD**, *not* 400 MAD. Sometimes, an officer may verbally quote "400 Dirhams" out of habit or to test if you know the tiers. Politely pointing to the radar readout and stating, *"Mon Adjudant, la vitesse retenue est inférieure à 20 km/h au-dessus de la limite, c'est une contravention de troisième classe à 150 Dirhams,"* immediately signals that you know Law 116-14 inside out.

callout.text: Exceeding the speed limit by 50 km/h or more (e.g., hitting 117 km/h in a 60 km/h village transition zone) is not an administrative ticket. Your physical driving license is confiscated on the spot, ATF discounts are void, and you must pay a judicial deposit of 4,000 MAD (€370) pending a court appearance.

sections.heading: Hardware on the Asphalt: Mesta Fusion Towers, TruCAM Lasers & Checkpoint Traps
sections.content:
To avoid fines altogether, you must recognize the three distinct layers of speed enforcement deployed across major hubs like [Casablanca](/locations/casablanca), [Rabat](/locations/rabat), [Marrakech](/locations/marrakech), and [Tangier](/locations/tanger).

### 1. Next-Gen Fixed Radars (Idemia Mesta Fusion 2)
Gone are the days of simple grey metal boxes that only flashed rear license plates in one lane. Since 2021, NARSA has deployed over 550 **Mesta Fusion 2** multi-target Doppler radar turrets—tall, sleek white-and-black vertical pillars mounted alongside highways and urban boulevards. 
* **Capabilities:** These towers track up to 32 vehicles simultaneously across 8 lanes at a range of 200 meters.
* **Bi-Directional:** They photograph both **approaching (front)** and **receding (rear)** traffic simultaneously. Slowing down only when the radar is facing your side of the road will get you flashed from across the median on two-lane national roads.
* **Multi-Infraction:** Beyond speed, high-resolution infrared cameras inside these pillars automatically detect vehicles running red lights, crossing solid white lane dividers, and driving on hard shoulders.

### 2. Mobile Laser Binoculars (LTI TruCAM II & Ultralyte)
Operated exclusively by the Royal Gendarmerie on national routes and highway interchanges, and by the DGSN inside cities, these tripod-mounted or handheld optical units are lethal to inattentive drivers.
* **Line-of-Sight Range:** A Gendarme standing under the shade of an overpass or behind an oleander bush in the highway median can lock onto your front license plate from **600 to 1,000 meters away**—long before your eyes can spot their grey uniform.
* **Photographic Proof:** Under Moroccan law, an officer cannot simply claim you were speeding based on visual estimation or an unrecorded radar gun. The modern TruCAM units record a high-definition video clip and still image stamped with GPS coordinates, date, time, target distance, measured speed, and retained speed. **You have the legal right to politely ask to view the screen (*voir la photo sur l'appareil*) to verify your license plate and recorded speed.**

### 3. The Classic Moroccan Trap: The '60–80–60' Village Funnel
The single highest-grossing revenue trap in Morocco occurs on National Roads (like the N8 between Marrakech and Beni Mellal, or the N2 near Chefchaouen). As you cruise legally at 100 km/h in your [Dacia Sandero Stepway](/vehicles/dacia-sandero-stepway), you will see an 80 km/h sign, followed just 150 meters later by a 60 km/h sign marking a small rural intersection. 

Most European drivers simply lift their foot off the accelerator, coasting down from 100 km/h to 78 km/h as they pass the 60 km/h sign. The Gendarmerie laser operator is positioned 100 meters past that 60 km/h sign. At 78 km/h (retained speed 72 km/h), you are clocked at 12 km/h over the limit. In Morocco, speed limit signs are **point-of-sign absolute**: you must complete your braking *before* the nose of your car crosses the vertical plane of the 60 km/h sign.

callout.text: Download Waze before picking up your vehicle. Fixed radars in Morocco are legally preceded by warning signs (Panneaux Radar), and Waze has 99% accuracy on fixed Mesta towers and roughly 85% real-time crowdsourced accuracy on Royal Gendarmerie mobile tripods.

sections.heading: The Roadside Audit: Step-by-Step Protocol & Demanding the Official 'Quittance'
sections.content:
When a Gendarme or police officer steps into the road and motions toward the shoulder with a whistle or red baton, how you handle the next three minutes dictates whether you leave with a clean legal transaction or become a target for informal solicitation.

### Step 1: The Approach & Decorum
Signal immediately, pull completely off the asphalt onto the gravel shoulder, turn on your hazard lights, roll down your window, and **stay inside the vehicle** unless asked to step out to inspect the radar screen. Keep your hands visible on the wheel. Greet the officer respectfully (*"Salam Alaikum, mon Commandant"* or *"Bonjour Monsieur l'agent"*). Never adopt an aggressive, entitled tone; Moroccan officers hold wide procedural discretion regarding vehicle safety inspections.

### Step 2: Document Presentation
Have your physical documents stored in the glovebox or door pocket—never in the trunk. Hand over:
1. Your original national driving license.
2. Your passport (so they can verify your tourist entry date).
